  `__tests__/integration/ops-owner-login.integration.spec.ts`.

## Phase X1.4 — forgot-password limit per address (XA-04)

- **Asset:** a person's mailbox and our email sending reputation; the reset-email flow's anti-enumeration property.
- **Actor → action → consequence (before):** anyone with many client IPs → `POST /auth/forgot-password` for one victim
  address from each IP → an unbounded number of password-reset emails to that victim (mail-bombing; reset tokens
  minted without limit; provider reputation burned). Only the per-IP route limit (`AUTH_THROTTLE`, 5/min/IP) applied.
- **Control:** `PasswordResetEmailLimiterService` (Twenty's `password-reset-email:<email>` bucket, 3 per 15 minutes,
  continuous refill), one atomic EVAL of the shared `TOKEN_BUCKET_SCRIPT` on the bounded auth-cache Redis client.
  `AuthService.doForgotPassword` calls it FIRST, for every submitted address, before any account lookup, token, outbox row
  or audit row. Key = sha256 of the trimmed, lower-cased address under `crewflow:{env}:password-reset-email:` (no email in
  Redis). A refusal writes nothing (an exhausted address's wait is never extended).
- **Enumeration:** the key, the decision and the 429 body (`PASSWORD_RESET_RATE_LIMITED`, constant, no retry time) depend
  only on the submitted string, never on whether an account exists; the 150 ms response floor pads the 429 too.
- **Failure policy:** Redis down → the route's `@RateLimitRequired` guard already answers 503 (CF-17, unchanged). A Redis
  error inside the limiter (guard call succeeded, limiter call failed) → 503 `RATE_LIMIT_UNAVAILABLE`: no token, no email.
  Never "send anyway".
- **Unchanged:** per-IP route limit, reset-token TTL (1 h) / hashing / single-use consume, CF-06 password-provider gate,
  outbox publish-after-commit.
- **Residual:** an attacker can spend a victim's 3 reset emails per 15 minutes, delaying the victim's own reset by up to
  ~5 minutes per token (continuous refill). Accepted as Twenty's trade-off; the values are code constants.
- **Tests:** `password-reset-email-limiter.service.spec.ts`, `forgot-password-email-limit.integration.spec.ts`
  (4 IPs → 3 emails then 429; 20 concurrent → ≤3; known = unknown status and body; per-IP limit kept).

## PERF — tenant framing: search_path and the Worker read-only flag folded into the binding SELECT (T-1, branch phase-x/t1-tenant-framing, PR #95, 2026-11-11, not merged)

**Change.** `TenantContextService.bindGucs` now sets `search_path` in the same `SELECT` as the identity GUCs when the
schema is known before the bind (HWS off; HWS on without a workspace; a replica read whose schema was validated on the
primary), as bound parameter `$6`, transaction-local. A new option `readOnly` adds
`set_config('transaction_read_only', 'on', true)` to that `SELECT`; the Worker's four hot read-only scans use it instead of
their own `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY` (ST-01/ST-02). API transactions: 6 → 5 framing statements; Worker scans: 7 → 5.

**Unchanged (owner decision P1-13):** both `RESET ROLE`s (G-09 layers 1 and 2) as their own statements; the
`current_user = session_user` assertion; Admin Inspect's first-statement `SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY` (CF-02); the replica
path's READ ONLY; the security snapshot's isolation statement; FORCE RLS; transaction-local context. A raw
`BEGIN READ ONLY` that bypasses TypeORM stays rejected (ST-03: it would end the outer transaction early).

**Threats considered.**
- *search_path list injection.* A bound value prevents SQL injection but not a comma-separated list (`'x, core'` is two
  schemas). Only `'core'` or a `workspaceSchemaName()` result that matched the registry is ever passed. ST-07 adds the same
  check on a Redis cache hit: a cached name that is not exactly the derived name is dropped and decided from Postgres
  (`name-mismatch` on any disagreement).
- *Read-only weakened.* It is stricter: it now applies from the binding `SELECT`, before any business statement (it used
  to follow setup). Writes fail with 25006 on PG16 and PG18, inside SAVEPOINTs too.
- *Context surviving the transaction.* All folded settings are `is_local = true`; proven to revert after COMMIT and
  ROLLBACK on the same pooled backend.
- *Pool poisoning (G-09).* Unchanged; re-proven with the folded statement, for the checkout hook and for layer 2 alone.

**Residual.** `request_complete.sqlCount` now includes the checkout `RESET ROLE` (ST-05); when the pool is full, that
count can be attributed to the request that released the connection. Statement counts for decisions come from
`pg_stat_statements` as `crewflow_owner`.

**Regression tests:** `tenant-context.service.spec.ts` (exact sequences, framing-count guard),
`tenant-context-framing.integration.spec.ts` (real PG, owner login, pool max 1: settings, revert, 25006, poisoned session,
injection), `schema-resolver.service.spec.ts` (ST-07), `session-role-reset.spec.ts` (ST-05).

## Phase X1.1 — security audit events, best effort (XR-01, owner decision 2026-11-12)

- **Asset:** the evidence trail of security actions under the one owner login (G-05/BC-07).
- **Before:** only `security.posture.drift` reached the sink (XR-01); logins, grants, role changes, payroll approvals and
  deletions existed only in `core.audit_log`, which the owner login can rewrite.
- **Control:** after commit, one BullMQ job per security audit row (ids only); the Worker re-reads the row under FORCE RLS
  and writes the redacted event to the configured sink with retries. Redaction: secret-looking keys and `name=value`
  pairs `[REDACTED]` (passwords, tokens, keys, private keys, JWTs, bearer/basic credentials, named one-time codes,
  connection strings), e-mails masked (Unicode-aware; a login-field value that is not a valid address ships as
  `[not-an-email]`, never the raw input), URLs replaced, length/depth bounded (~16 KB per event). The frozen
  privileged-copy migration never ships (owner decision 2026-11-12).
- **Failed-login events are dropped above a 10,000 backlog** (owner decision 2026-11-12): the pre-authentication failed
  login (no organisation, no audit row) is queued fire-and-forget as a system-scoped audit job; when the audit queue's
  backlog (waiting + delayed + prioritized, read at most every 2 s per process) is over 10,000, new failed-login events are
  dropped and counted — a process counter plus a durable Redis total on one dedicated key, shown on the platform-admin
  Health tab ("Security audit events"). A failed login never waits on or fails because of the audit path. Other audit
  events are never dropped by this guard.
- **Fail-open by design:** a Redis, queue or sink failure never blocks, delays or rolls back an action (Twenty's
  event-log model). A rolled-back transaction ships nothing (publisher discard + the Worker's re-read).
- **Abuse cases tested:** forged scope / cross-tenant payload ships nothing; forged id pairs under real RLS ship nothing;
  extra payload keys (action, e-mail) refused before Redis; a malformed job fails without a retry or a read; a raw
  savepoint rollback ships nothing; a hung or failing pre-auth add never changes the login response, status or timing
  class.
- **Residual:** see G-05 and Residual risks (events lost on Redis/sink failure; rows alterable before shipping; savepoint
  discard; address-shaped passwords; unquoted `&`; failed-login drops under a flood).
- **Tests:** `security-audit-event-catalogue.spec.ts` (incl. the repo-wide raw audit_log insert scan),
  `build-security-audit-event.spec.ts`, `redaction.spec.ts`, `audit-event-queue.service.spec.ts`,
  `audit-event-shipping.spec.ts`, `outbox-operations.replay-audit-event.spec.ts`, `queue-registry.spec.ts` (X1.1 block),
  `audit-event.handler.spec.ts`, `account-invite-cleanup.audit-events.spec.ts`,
  `audit-events-delivery.integration.spec.ts` (E1–E7).

## Phase X1.8 — test database isolation fails closed (cleanup audit DBT-01, DBT-02, DBT-10, DBT-12, XD-03; PR #27)

- **Asset:** the development database and any non-test database reachable from a developer machine; the disposable test
  cluster's bootstrap superuser credential. **Actor:** not an attacker: a developer `.env`, a shell export or a harness
  that hands the wrong environment to a test or e2e process (the 2026-10-05 incident class the guard exists for).
- **DBT-01 (reproduced 2026-11-02, disposable `rab_x1_int` + an unreachable decoy):** with `packages/rab-server/.env` =
  `NODE_ENV=development` + a decoy `DATABASE_URL` (127.0.0.1:1), `nx test rab-server` passed globalSetup (the TEST pair was
  valid) and then 1,089 application connection attempts went to the decoy: Nx loads `.env` into the task without
  overriding, the Nx Jest executor and Jest only default `NODE_ENV` when it is unset, and `applyIntegrationTestDatabaseEnv`
  returned early for any NODE_ENV but `test`, while fixtures used the TEST admin URL. CI was not affected (`NODE_ENV: test`).
- **Control (`test-database-guard.ts`):** the guard no longer depends on `NODE_ENV=test`. Under Jest any NODE_ENV but `test`
  (unset included) is refused in every test file (setupFiles, `JEST_WORKER_ID` set) and in globalSetup
  (`resolveForJestGlobalSetup`); outside Jest a non-test NODE_ENV stays inert, so runtime and CLI processes are unchanged.
  The database rules themselves never read NODE_ENV. Refused: the development database (rab-devdb 127.0.0.1:15432 on any
  loopback alias, compose host `devdb`, or the `DEVDB_URL` database); an inherited `PG_DATABASE_URL`,
  `PG_OPS_APP_DATABASE_URL` or `CREWFLOW_*_DATABASE_URL` naming another database or another login (DBT-02; empty = unset;
  the working directory's `.env` and `DOTENV_CONFIG_PATH` are read as data so a value @nestjs/config would load later is
  checked too); a non-empty `DATABASE_DIRECT_URL` or `PG_DATABASE_REPLICA_URL`; target-changing libpq variables (`PGHOST`,
  `PGPORT`, `PGUSER`, `PGDATABASE`, ...); a percent-encoded host; a TEST URL without its login; `TEST_DATABASE_CREWFLOW_URL`
  / `TEST_DATABASE_WORKER_URL` on another database (DBT-10). The catalog disposable marker and the same-cluster probe are
  unchanged. Messages carry variable names, host, port and database only. `seed-ai-e2e.ts` refuses a null routing.
- **XD-03 (`rab-worker/.../helpers/worker-login-env.ts`):** the Phase D worker-login switch copied
  `TEST_DATABASE_WORKER_URL` into `DATABASE_URL` unchecked. It now calls `applyWorkerLoginTestDatabaseEnv`, which, whatever
  NODE_ENV says, requires the valid TEST pair, the worker URL on the TEST database with its own login and no redirecting
  inherited URL or libpq variable, and refuses an `options` query parameter on the worker URL and the logins of
  `TEST_DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED`, `MIGRATION_SECURITY_ADMIN_URL` and `TEST_DATABASE_CREWFLOW_URL` (compared by name);
  nothing is changed on refusal. When the switch is on, the worker Jest globalSetup also connects as the worker login
  (`assertWorkerLoginNotPrivilegedAtRuntime`) and refuses when that login (`session_user`) is, or is a member (direct or
  inherited, `pg_has_role(session_user, r.oid, 'MEMBER')`) of, any superuser or BYPASSRLS role, or does not reach the
  TEST database.
- **DBT-12 (`run-ai-e2e.sh`):** the API, the rab-ai consumer, Vite and Playwright start through `runtime-env.sh`
  (`ai_e2e_runtime_exec` / `ai_e2e_client_exec`), which remove from the child: every `TEST_DATABASE_*` URL,
  `MIGRATION_SECURITY_ADMIN_URL`, the role bootstrap passwords, the legacy URLs, `DOTENV_CONFIG_PATH` and command authority;
  every libpq `PG*` name (`PGPASSWORD`, ...), every `PG_*URL` but `PG_DATABASE_URL`, every `POSTGRES_*` name; and any name
  whose value equals the superuser URL or `MIGRATION_SECURITY_ADMIN_URL`, or contains their password (8+ characters; the
  password and the value are each compared as written and percent-decoded; a URL scheme is ignored for this match). Names
  are read from `env -0`, so names bash cannot use as variables (e.g. `ADMIN.URL`) are covered. Clients also lose
  `PG_DATABASE_URL` and
  `APP_SECRET`. Only the seed keeps the admin connection. The harness refuses to start when `PG_DATABASE_URL` itself holds
  the admin credential, and runs the API and Worker in a fresh empty directory (`AI_E2E_WORK/runtime-cwd.*`, proved free of
  `.env`), so an env file kept as `AI_E2E_WORK/.env` is never loaded by ConfigModule.
- **Regression tests:** `test-database-guard.spec.ts` (the database rules refuse the development database by their own rule
  for NODE_ENV unset / empty / development / production / staging; the worker-login switch is refused for the development
  database, another database, a remote host, a missing TEST pair, no login, the superuser / migration-admin / crewflow
  logins, an `options` query parameter and redirecting env; the live privilege check runs against the real TEST database
  and refuses a superuser login and a non-superuser login that is a member of a superuser role);
  `run-ai-e2e-env.test.cjs` runs the REAL `run-ai-e2e.sh` with `node` / `curl` / `powershell.exe` stubbed on PATH and
  asserts on every spawned child's environment (unknown children fail): the superuser credential as URL, `postgresql://`,
  `?sslmode=`, `localhost`, keyword string, `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`, inherited `PGPASSWORD`, an encoded source password, a raw
  source password with a percent-encoded copy, a bash-invalid name (`ADMIN.URL`) and an `AI_E2E_WORK/.env` file all reach
  the seed only. Wired into `ci-e2e` spec-coverage.
- **Residual:** a developer who sets `NODE_ENV=test` and points `TEST_DATABASE_URL` at a real database that also carries
  `crewflow.disposable_test_database = 'true'` is not stopped (the marker is the positive opt-in, by design). The devdb
  endpoint list is the repository's own compose shape. `runtime-env.sh` is a deny-list (an allow-list was not taken: the
  real harness cannot be exercised in review, and it would drop platform / env-file variables the children need): a NEW
  credential that is not listed, not `PG*` / `POSTGRES_*` and does not carry an 8+ character admin password still reaches
  the children; an admin password shorter than 8 characters is matched only as the exact URL value.

## X1.6 — Redis is protected by the private Docker network only, as in Twenty (branch phase-x2/x16-redis-port-gate, 2026-11-12, PR #111)

Owner decision 2026-11-12 (Phase X Part 2, "the Twenty way", §2): Twenty has no Redis authentication mechanism, so
Crewflow adds none. No Redis setting changes. Twenty reference: `packages/twenty-docker/docker-compose.yml` (the `redis`
service: no `ports:`, no password, `--maxmemory-policy noeviction`).

- **Asset:** everything in Redis: BullMQ jobs, schedulers and locks (email, push, pay statements, timer triggers, scans),
  rate-limit and throttle counters, the auth-context and entity caches, realtime Pub/Sub, Worker health stats.
- **Actor:** anyone who can open a TCP connection to the Redis port.
- **Accepted risk:** `docker-compose.production.yml` runs Redis with no password and no ACL (AOF + `noeviction` only).
  Anyone who reaches it can read job payloads (ids, no secrets), add, delete or forge BullMQ jobs, clear throttles and
  rate limits, poison caches, or stop scheduled work. Consumers check forged ids against committed, tenant-scoped rows
  and refuse unknown job names, but a forged job can still trigger a send or scan earlier or again. Reach is limited to
  the private Docker network of the stack: the containers of that Compose project and anything else an operator attaches
  to it. `docker-compose.image.yml` keeps its ACL and `maxmemory`; this entry does not weaken it.
- **Control (gate):** `packages/rab-docker/scripts/compose-one-image.cjs` refuses, in every deploy combination
  (`production.yml`; `image.yml`, alone and with `local-db`, `staging` and the rehearsal overlay) and in
  `docker-compose.local-build.yml`, any Redis service that has `ports:` in short or long syntax (loopback included), a
  `network_mode`, or a network that resolves to the host network or uses a host / macvlan / ipvlan driver; and any other
  service in a Redis network namespace (`network_mode: service:<redis>`). `expose:` is refused too, as a review-hygiene
  rule (it publishes nothing). A Redis service is recognised by name or image, by a `redis-server` / `redis-cli`
  command, entrypoint or health check, or as the host of the app's committed `REDIS_URL`. Before X1.6 no gate checked
  `production.yml`'s Redis ports. Tests: `compose-one-image.test.cjs` (pure and rendered denials).
- **Control (runtime):** the Worker's bullmq preflight still refuses any eviction policy other than `noeviction`. An
  unauthenticated `REDIS_URL` is logged as a warning that states this accepted risk. No release will turn it into a
  refusal.
- **Operator rule:** never publish the Redis port, never put Redis on the host network, and never attach untrusted
  containers to the stack's network. A platform that cannot keep Redis on a private network must use
  `docker-compose.image.yml` (ACL file) or a managed Redis with auth.
- **Residual (accepted by the owner, 2026-11-12):**
  - any process on the Docker network, or a compromised container in the stack, has full read and write access to Redis;
  - a forwarder in another service (for example a `socat`-style proxy, `tcp-listen:6379` → `tcp:rab-redis:6379`) that
    publishes its own port is not recognised as Redis and passes the gate. Refusing it would need a deny-by-default
    port allowlist for every service, a new mechanism the owner has not chosen;
  - a Redis with no redis-named image or command that the app does not name in a committed `REDIS_URL` is not
    recognised either (same reason);
  - the gate checks only the committed compose files: a hand-edited server file, an operator `docker run -p`, or a
    platform that publishes container ports on its own is outside it.

  This closes the "Revisit: before production stage D" note of the Lane A trade-off (unauthenticated Redis is a
  warning, not a refusal, in bullmq mode).

## X1.3 — `seed` / `seed-qa` have no in-command refusal of staging or production targets (accepted risk; cleanup audit XA-03 / NC-04, PR #29 closed)

Owner decision 2026-11-12 (Phase X Part 2, "the Twenty way"): no code change. Running a fixture seed against production
is an operator error, as in Twenty. PR #29 (`x1/seed-guards`, head `cced3aad`, titled "X1.5" under the cleanup audit's
numbering) had the fix. It was closed unmerged on 2026-11-15. This entry changes no code. File:line references are to
the code at this PR's base.

- **Asset:** the integrity of a deployed database: who is a platform administrator, which organisations and accounts exist.
- **Actor → action → consequence:** an operator (or anyone holding the owner login plus `DB_TARGET=production` and
  `ALLOW_PRODUCTION_DB_COMMANDS=true`) runs `seed` or `seed-qa` against a production database by mistake. The effects:
  - `seed` writes the permission catalogue (idempotent), an organisation (`SEED_ORG_SLUG`, default `acme`), a
    `super_admin` role holding every permission, and an ACTIVE user (`SEED_ADMIN_EMAIL`, default `admin@acme.test`) with
    the operator-supplied password. It also writes a `core.platform_admin` row for that user (`command/seed.command.ts:45`,
    `:123-128`), so a new platform administrator exists in the live database.
  - `seed-qa` writes the `adolphus-qa` fixture organisation and `*.qa@example.test` users that share one password.

  Cleanup audit rating: priority P0, severity LOW–MEDIUM. It needs operator authority, and it is an integrity and cleanup
  problem, not a disclosure.
- **What is missing:** a refusal inside the two commands. `seed-ai-demo` has one (`seed-ai-demo.command.ts:42`, refuses
  any `DB_TARGET` but `local`).
  - `seed` checks nothing before writing. Its first transaction inserts any missing permission keys, and the `acme`
    organisation is inserted next (`seed.command.ts:46-65`). Only then does it check `SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD`
    (`:69-71`). A run refused for a missing password can therefore already have written the catalogue and the
    organisation.
  - `seed-qa` checks its password and that `--admin-email` is present (`seed-qa.command.ts:102-108`), then writes missing
    permission keys (`:114-119`). Only after that does it check that the address is an active platform administrator
    (`:325`, refusal at `:354`). Its own comment "Every refusal comes before the first write" (`:100`) is not accurate
    for the catalogue.
  - The only target check is the generic CLI gate (`command/main.ts:28`, `assertDbTarget('command')`), which allows
    production.
- **Why accepted:** anyone who can pass the production gates below already holds the `crewflow_owner` login, which can
  write the same rows directly. The guard would stop mistakes, not attackers. Twenty has no such guard, and the owner
  chose not to add a Crewflow-only mechanism.
- **Compensating controls (in the code at this PR's base):**
  - **What production needs.** A production CLI command needs only `DB_TARGET=production` and
    `ALLOW_PRODUCTION_DB_COMMANDS=true` from the process environment (`database/typeorm/core/database-target.ts:181-187`),
    plus the owner login.
    - Both are refused when they come from a `.env` file that Nx loads (`:203-213`).
    - The deployment identity (`CREWFLOW_DEPLOYMENT_ENVIRONMENT` / `CREWFLOW_DEPLOYMENT_ID`) is **optional** in production
      since owner decision BC-11, 2026-11-05 (`database/deployment-identity/deployment-identity.ts:147-149`, `:356-367`).
      When declared, it must say production and match the database's live marker. When undeclared, the marker check is
      skipped with a warning.
    - The `database-target.ts:9-15` header still lists the deployment id as required. That header is stale; correcting it
      is a code follow-up, not part of this entry.
  - **Authority is per-invocation in the image.**
    - The owner-login env lint refuses `ALLOW_PRODUCTION_DB_COMMANDS`, `DB_TARGET` and `ALLOW_REMOTE_TEST_DATABASE` in
      runtime and database env files (`packages/rab-docker/scripts/compose-owner-login.cjs:156`).
    - `api-prestart.sh` hands `DB_TARGET` / `ALLOW_PRODUCTION_DB_COMMANDS` only to a one-off command with arguments
      (`docker compose run -e`), and refuses them on the API start (`packages/rab-docker/rab/api-prestart.sh:175-193`;
      tests 13d/13e, `rab/api-prestart-test/run-prestart-shell-tests.cjs:607-612`).
    - Exception: `packages/rab-docker/.env.migrate.example:22-25` sets `DB_TARGET=production`,
      `ALLOW_PRODUCTION_DB_COMMANDS=true` and the deployment identity persistently, for the one-off `rab-migrate` service
      only. That file is never passed to rab-api or rab-worker; `compose-credential-isolation.cjs` checks this.
  - **Staging, local and test targets.**
    - `DB_TARGET=staging` is refused for every command (`database-target.ts:225-227`).
    - `local` and `test` refuse a dotted remote host (`:229-232`). Exception: `DB_TARGET=test` with
      `ALLOW_REMOTE_TEST_DATABASE=true` allows a remote host (`:230`).
    - An undeclared non-production process refuses a database whose marker is bound to production
      (`deployment-identity.ts:432-436`). A database bound to staging or test passes with a warning only (`:438-439`).
  - **Owner login.** The CLI boot gates require `crewflow_owner` for every CLI command, before Nest boots
    (`command/main.ts:32`, `runDatabaseBootGates('cli')` in `database/boot-checks/database-boot-gates.ts`).
  - **No default passwords.** `seed` needs `SEED_ADMIN_PASSWORD` (`seed.command.ts:69-71`) and `seed-qa` needs
    `SEED_QA_PASSWORD` (`seed-qa.command.ts:102-105`), each at least 12 characters. `seed-qa` also needs an active
    platform administrator (`:325`, `:354`).
  - **No deploy path runs either command.** A `git grep` of `packages/rab-docker` finds only two test harnesses that run
    `seed-qa`, each against its own disposable database: `staging/rehearsal/run-image-rehearsal.cjs:439` and
    `rab/runtime-isolation-test/run-h6-runtime.cjs:384`.
- **Residual:** an operator who passes `DB_TARGET=production` and `ALLOW_PRODUCTION_DB_COMMANDS=true` for some other
  one-off command, then types `seed` or `seed-qa`, gets fixture rows and (with `seed`) a platform administrator in
  production. The same applies, with no production authority at all, to a remote `test` database opened with
  `ALLOW_REMOTE_TEST_DATABASE=true` and to an undeclared staging- or test-bound database. The cleanup is manual: remove
  the platform-admin row, the user, the role and the organisation.
- **Revisit when any of these happens:**
  - a deploy, start, upgrade or CI step, or a runbook, runs `seed` / `seed-qa` against a deployed database;
  - a staging command path is added (`DB_TARGET=staging` is no longer refused);
  - `ALLOW_REMOTE_TEST_DATABASE=true` is used against anything but a disposable database;
  - a deployed staging or test database runs without a declared deployment identity (only a warning protects it);
  - production command authority becomes persistent in a rab-api / rab-worker environment, or someone other than the
    owner holds it;
  - seed fixture rows turn up in a deployed database. The check:
    `SELECT id, slug FROM core.organisation WHERE slug IN ('acme', 'adolphus-qa');` and
    `SELECT id, email FROM core."user" WHERE email LIKE '%@acme.test' OR email LIKE '%.qa@example.test';`. Run them in a
    session that RLS lets see every organisation. A session with no tenant context sees zero rows by design, which is
    not a clean result;
  - Twenty adds such a guard.

  Re-opening PR #29 (`seed-target-guard.ts`) is the prepared fix. It must be re-tested under the single `crewflow_owner`
  login.

## X1.5 — system mail driver: SMTP STARTTLS on port 587 is opportunistic; production does not refuse `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS=true` (accepted risk; XR-04)

Owner decision 2026-11-12 (Phase X Part 2, "the Twenty way"): no change to the **system mail driver**
(`engine/core-modules/email/email-driver.factory.ts`, the environment-configured transport that sends every
platform email). Twenty's system driver does the same: its `email-driver.factory.ts` declares `requireTLS` in its
options type and never sets it. It sets only `secure: false` and `ignoreTLS: true` when `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS` is on
(checked against `twentyhq/twenty` on 2026-11-15). The acceptance covers only this driver. The planned X1.5a proof test
(a STARTTLS-less SMTP sink) and the X1.5b fix were not done. This entry changes no code. File:line references are to the
code at this PR's base.

- **Asset:** the SMTP relay credentials (`EMAIL_SMTP_USER` / `EMAIL_SMTP_PASSWORD`), and the password-reset, activation
  and invitation links (bearer secrets until used or expired) in every message.
- **Actor → action → consequence:** an on-path attacker between the host and the SMTP relay strips the relay's
  `STARTTLS` capability from the EHLO reply → nodemailer, with no `requireTLS`, carries on in clear → the attacker reads
  the AUTH exchange (relay credentials: send-as-us, reputation) and the message bodies (take over an account by using a
  reset or invite link first). If an operator sets `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS=true` in production, the same happens with no
  attacker work, and nothing refuses it. The XR-04 audit marked this as suspected: nodemailer upgrades only when STARTTLS
  is advertised, unless `requireTLS` is set, but the strip was never run against our transport.
- **Where (system driver):** `email-driver.factory.ts:37` sets `secure: !noTls && port === 465`, `:38` sets
  `ignoreTLS: noTls`, and `requireTLS` is never set. `email/drivers/smtp.driver.ts:124` passes these options to
  `nodemailer.createTransport`; the Worker sends through the same `EmailService`. The two SMTP health probes copy the
  same options but send no credentials: `platform-admin/admin-panel.service.ts:300-305` and `admin-health.service.ts:241-246`.
  `productionConfigurationProblems` in `env.validation.ts` has no `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS` rule. The templates default to port
  587: `packages/rab-docker/env/runtime.env.example:42` and the staging `api.env.example:33` / `worker.env.example:30`.
- **Known issue, NOT accepted here — the Admin Panel "Test Connection"** (`platform-admin/admin-panel.service.ts:242-248`).
  The owner accepted only the system driver. Twenty's user-chosen STARTTLS path sets `requireTLS: true`
  (`imap-smtp-caldav-connection/utils/build-smtp-tls-options.util.ts`). Ours has two gaps:
  - In `starttls` mode, Test Connection builds the transport with no `requireTLS`. It can send the stored SMTP password,
    so a strip exposes it.
  - In `none` mode (`ignoreTLS: true`), the stored, decrypted SMTP password is sent in clear to whatever host and port
    the platform admin names.

  Both are tracked for a lead fix PR. This entry does not widen the acceptance to them.
- **Why accepted (system driver only):** this matches Twenty's system driver. Setting `requireTLS` would stop all mail on
  a relay that offers no STARTTLS, and the production relay's STARTTLS support has not been confirmed (the X1.5b
  precondition). The cost of an attack is not negligible, and this is not a closed network: a hosted VM talking to a
  separately hosted relay crosses transit networks the project does not control. Exploiting the strip needs an active
  on-path position on that path, not just passive capture. The owner accepted that exposure for now.
- **Compensating controls:**
  - When STARTTLS is offered and not stripped, nodemailer upgrades, and Node verifies the relay certificate by default.
    A `git grep rejectUnauthorized` over `packages/rab-server/src/engine/core-modules/email`,
    `packages/rab-server/src/engine/core-modules/platform-admin` and `packages/rab-worker/src` finds no non-test hit, so
    nothing turns verification off on these paths.
  - `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS` defaults to `false` (`environment-variables.ts:1541`, `packages/rab-server/.env.example:117`).
  - Production refuses `EMAIL_DRIVER=LOGGER` (`env.validation.ts:298`), so links are never written to logs instead.
  - Every token is single-use and hashed at rest (SHA-256, `password-reset-token.service.ts:19-20`), so a captured link
    is worth something only until it is used or expires. Lifetimes:
    - self-service forgot-password: 1 hour (`auth.service.ts:1042`);
    - admin reset: 48 hours (the service default, `password-reset-token.service.ts:9` and `:50`, issued at
      `account-lifecycle.service.ts:181-185`);
    - initial setup: the same 48-hour default would apply, but no code at this PR's base issues that purpose;
    - account invites: 24 hours, up to 3 sends (`account-invite.service.ts:8-10`).
  - **Operator rule:** to remove the strip entirely, use port 465 (implicit TLS: `secure` is set, and TLS is negotiated
    before any SMTP command) or `EMAIL_DRIVER=RESEND` (HTTPS API). Never set `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS=true` outside local
    development.
- **Residual:** on 587, an active on-path attacker can downgrade to cleartext and capture the relay credentials and
  in-flight links. `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS=true` in production sends everything in clear, and no gate refuses it.
- **Revisit when any of these happens:**
  - production moves to its final hosting, or the relay or host provider changes: re-assess the host-to-relay path and
    the relay's STARTTLS support then;
  - the production relay is confirmed to offer STARTTLS (that removes the only objection to `requireTLS` for 587, so
    X1.5b can ship);
  - `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS=true` turns up in any deployed environment;
  - an SMTP credential leak or a reset-link takeover is suspected;
  - Twenty's system driver starts setting `requireTLS`;
  - the system driver (`engine/core-modules/email/email-driver.factory.ts`) changes its TLS options, or the Admin
    Panel's stored SMTP configuration starts sending real mail (today only Test Connection uses it).

  The prepared fix is the X1.5a sink test, then `requireTLS: true` in `email-driver.factory.ts` when
  `!noTls && !secure`, plus a production refusal of `EMAIL_SMTP_NO_TLS=true` (env-validation diff to the lead).

## XA-08 — the forgot-password address is handed over in router state, never the URL (branch phase-x2/x62-forgot-email-router-state, 2026-11-12, PR #112)

Phase X Part 2 finding XA-08 (`docs/plans/PHASE-X-STAGE0-PART2.md` §2.6). Front only: no server, env or header change.

- **Asset:** the e-mail address a person typed on the sign-in screen (or their own address on Settings → Security).
  **Actor:** anyone with read access to browser history/sync, a server, CDN or proxy access log, an analytics tool, or a
  third-party page receiving a `Referer` (`Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` is set only in `rab-front/vercel.json`).
- **Before:** `Login.tsx` ("Forgot password?") and `PasswordCard.tsx` ("Reset password") linked to
  `/forgot-password?email=<address>`, and `ForgotPassword.tsx` pre-filled the field from that query string.
- **Control:** both links pass `{ email }` as react-router state; `ForgotPassword` pre-fills only from a string
  `location.state.email` and no longer reads `?email=` (a legacy link opens with an empty field). The address is in no
  URL, so it reaches no access log, history entry or Referer. The pre-filled field (the UX) is unchanged.
- **Tests:** `ForgotPasswordEmailHandover.spec.tsx`: from both entry points the field is pre-filled and the address
  (raw or encoded) is in no `pathname`/`search`/`hash` the router ever held; a legacy `?email=` and non-string state are
  ignored. Fails 3 of 5 on the previous code.
- **Residual:** router state lives in `history.state`, which a browser may keep in its session-restore data on the
  device; it is never sent over the network.

## Phase X3.2: server errors to Sentry through an exception handler (Twenty's exception-handler module)

### P0-sentry addendum (X3.2): 500s and failed Worker cycles are now reported; nothing new leaves the process
- **Asset:** the same as P0-sentry: session cookies, `Authorization` headers, request bodies (passwords, reset and
  activation tokens, MFA codes), refresh tokens, TOTP secrets and recovery codes, email addresses.
  **Actor → action → consequence considered:** anyone with access to the third-party Sentry project reads those values
  from a reported server error; or a Sentry outage or SDK fault changes an API response or stops the Worker.
- **Before:** the API's unhandled-exception branch (`engine/filters/all-exceptions.filter.ts`) and the Worker cycle catch
  (`core/runtime/worker-runtime.ts`) only logged; 5xx never reached Sentry (audit XR-03). Only uncaught exceptions,
  unhandled rejections and the provisioning-health `captureMessage` did.
- **Control:** `engine/core-modules/exception-handler/` (Twenty's exception-handler module, re-implemented):
  `ExceptionHandlerService` over one driver, the Sentry driver when `SENTRY_DSN` is set and `instrument.ts` initialised a
  client, otherwise a no-op driver. Called from the generic 500 branch of `AllExceptionsFilter` only (every 4xx branch
  returns first; `shouldCaptureException` refuses an `HttpException` < 500) and from the Worker cycle catch (same
  predicate). Every event still leaves through the P0-sentry `beforeSend` (request headers, cookies, body, query string
  and env deleted; user reduced to its opaque id; JWTs, bearer values, `password=` / `token=` / `secret=` values and
  emails redacted; dropped if scrubbing throws). What the handler itself adds is fixed: the operation kind and a data-free
  name (HTTP method + Express route pattern, or the Worker loop name). It copies nothing off the exception object. The
  scrubbers' sensitive-key list now also covers MFA enrolment fields whose names it missed (`otpauthUri`, `manualKey`,
  `qrDataUrl`, `recoveryCodes` / `backupCodes`, `totpCode`), free-text redaction also catches camelCase / snake_case
  credential names (`newPassword=`, `refreshToken:`, `"currentPassword":`, `"accessToken":`, `"mfaCode":`, `totpCode`,
  `recoveryCode`), URL-encoded emails (`bob%40example.com`, also in an otpauth label) and connection strings whose
  password contains `@` (stricter only; every pattern stays bounded and linear). Body-parser client errors (oversized
  body, unsupported charset or content-encoding) are thrown before any guard or throttler, so they are
  answered with their 4xx and a fixed body and are never reported: an unauthenticated caller cannot flood Sentry with
  them or get an attacker-chosen charset name into an event (they used to be a generic 500). Reporting is best effort: the service and
  both callers swallow any driver or SDK error, so the 500 body, the cycle outcome, its failure counter and the next cycle
  are unchanged, and Sentry's transport sends asynchronously.
- **Tests:** `all-exceptions.filter.http.spec.ts` (real HTTP, Nest default body parser: 200 KB body → 413, attacker
  charset → 415 without echo, `content-encoding: evil-enc` → 415, malformed JSON → 400 (unchanged), none reported; a real
  500 still reported), `exception-handler.service.spec.ts` (a 500 through the real filter → Sentry driver → the production
  `beforeSend` → an in-memory transport: no header, cookie, body, token, password, email or MFA value in the envelope;
  4xx sends nothing; no DSN / no client → no-op; a rejecting transport and a throwing SDK leave the response unchanged),
  `all-exceptions.filter.spec.ts` (500 calls the handler with the route pattern; nine 4xx/404/409/503 paths do not; a
  throwing handler or hostile request object leaves the 500 body unchanged), `worker-runtime.exception-handler.spec.ts`
  (failed cycle reported in both stats modes and interval mode; succeeded/idle/skipped and client errors not; a throwing
  handler leaves outcome, failure count, next cycle unchanged with no unhandled rejection; default with no DSN is a
  no-op), `instrument.spec.ts` (MFA fields filtered; MFA status counts kept).
- **Residual:** the error message (free text) and stack frames are sent, redacted by pattern only; a secret in a message
  that matches no pattern is sent — in particular a BARE recovery or TOTP code with no key name next to it ("recovery
  code ABCD-EFGH", "totp 482913"). The event's `request.url` and `transaction` keep the raw request PATH (query string and
  fragment removed): today those path segments are internal UUIDs only, but a future route with an email, token or other
  personal value in the path would send it (review F4, not fixed in this PR). Thrown `HttpException`s with status >= 500
  are not reported (owner text: the 500 branch only). Exception events carry the scrubbed request URL path (path
  segments are kept, as in P0-sentry). No user or organisation is attached to these events.

## /healthz databaseLogin — the health check notices a refused runtime login (branch fix/api-health-db-login, 2026-11-13, PR #133)
- **Asset:** availability signal of the API; the runtime login `crewflow_owner`.
- **Before:** /healthz only pinged through the pool (`SELECT 1` on an existing connection), so a changed or revoked login stayed
  invisible until the pool needed a new connection (observed live in the #125 deliberate-password-change test).
- **Control:** a new indicator opens ONE fresh runtime-login connection through the connection factory (same target, login,
  TLS and startup options as the runtime pool; read-only session; `application_name` ending `-health`), runs `SELECT 1`,
  closes it. Single flight; result (up or down) cached 5 s on a monotonic clock; connect 2.5 s / query 1.5 s / whole probe 3 s.
  Response: `status` plus the fixed text "database login failed" only (no URL, login, SQLSTATE or driver message); one log
  line per state change with the SQLSTATE only. The connection budget counts one probe connection per API instance.
- **Accepted signal:** /healthz is public and unauthenticated, so a caller can now tell "database reachable but the runtime
  login is refused" from "database down" (owner decision: notice lost logins). It reveals when credentials are rotated or
  revoked, nothing more.
- **Residual:** under severe CPU starvation the 3 s deadline can briefly report the login down (compose marks the container
  unhealthy only after 15 consecutive failures; `restart: unless-stopped` does not restart unhealthy containers). Behind a
  transaction pooler with its own auth file, client auth can succeed on a stale password; only the primary endpoint is probed.
- **Tests:** `database-login.health.spec.ts` (up; 28P01 with no leak; query failure; factory refusal fails closed; deadline;
  single flight under 25 concurrent; cache up/down; clock jump backwards re-probes), connection-budget spec (probe slots),
  `healthz-database-login.integration.spec.ts` (password changed → 503 while the pooled ping is up; NOLOGIN; burst of 50
  opens one login; read-only `-health` session).

## X3.5-S7 / DEAD-07 — the test admin URL is renamed, and no integration suite can skip silently (branches cleanup/x35-s7-test-admin-url, cleanup/x35-dead07-helper, 2026-11-13, PRs #126 and #127)
- **Asset:** the disposable test cluster's bootstrap SUPERUSER URL (fixtures, identity probes, in-Jest migrations), and
  the guarantee that the RLS / tenant / payroll integration suites actually run.
- **S7 (release 1):** the admin URL is `TEST_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL`. The old name `TEST_DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED` is still
  accepted.
  - Two different values are refused, compared as written, names only.
  - Every X1.8 / X1.9 rule applies to whichever name supplied it.
  - setupFiles writes the validated value under both names, so a later dotenv load cannot add a second value.
  - The Worker-login switch refuses the admin login under either name.
  - Every committed child-process strip list removes both names. A static spec checks this, and both CI helpers emit both
    names with one value.
  - Abuse cases: `test-database-guard.spec.ts` (X3.5-S7 block), `test-database-admin-url-names.spec.ts`,
    `run-ai-e2e-env.test.cjs` (the new name and an alias of its value reach the AI e2e seed only).
- **DEAD-07:** ~280 specs used to skip when the legacy primary URL was absent. Under Jest that branch was dead, but a
  routing change (S6 / S8) would have turned every RLS, tenant and payroll suite into a silent skip.
  - They now gate on `integrationTestDatabaseReady()`, which throws (never returns false) unless NODE_ENV=test and the
    validated TEST pair are present.
  - An AST scan fails CI if any spec skip-conditional depends on a routing connection name again
    (`integration-test-database-gate.spec.ts`).
- **Spec-spawned runtime children** (`runtimeChildBaseEnv`, provisioner / Worker / API spawned by worker specs) no longer
  inherit either admin name, any `TEST_DATABASE_*` URL, `DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED`, `MIGRATION_SECURITY_ADMIN_URL`, the role
  bootstrap / owner / migrator passwords, or any variable holding an admin URL's password; a spec re-adds the one URL a child
  needs after the base (`runtime-child-env.spec.ts`).
- **Specs take the admin URL from the validated pair** (`integrationTestDatabase().adminUrl`), never from the environment;
  a scan fails CI on any spec or test helper reading `TEST_DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED`, `TEST_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL` or
  `DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED` from `process.env` (aliases, destructuring and computed keys included).
- **Residual:** `rab-worker/.../helpers/email-process-child.cjs:33` (a forked fixture child) still reads the legacy
  `DATABASE_URL_UNPOOLED` the Jest guard writes; it moves with S6 (the parent passes the admin URL explicitly).
- **Release 2 (S8):** the old name is refused; the strip lists keep both names permanently.

- **X2.4 Admin Panel health indicators (2026-11-12).** Actor: a signed-in non-platform-admin → `GET
  /rest/v1/admin/health/report` → 403 (PlatformAdminGuard, then `assertActivePlatformAdmin` in the service for direct
  callers); no audit row and no probe. A platform admin sees: API version/commit/Node/uptime, database connections vs
  max_connections (from `pg_stat_database`, cluster-wide), Redis version and memory (`INFO server` / `INFO memory`),
  per-queue BullMQ counts, scheduler counts. No tenant data, no host names, no URLs, no raw error text (fixed strings;
  a failing probe says "Not reachable."). Every Redis call is a read command (tested against `COMMAND INFO` flags);
  the report cache moved from Redis `SET EX` to process memory. Access audited as `admin.health_viewed` in the admin's
  organisation: at most once per admin per API process every 5 minutes, plus every manual Refresh (owner assumption,
  see the PR; at most one refresh row per admin per 5 s). A process restart resets the dedupe. The audit write is
  bounded at 2 s and fails closed (best-effort is an open owner decision). `?refresh=1` re-probes only a report at
  least 5 s old, through one shared in-flight probe set, so refreshes cannot multiply probes. The
  `admin.health_viewed` rows are NOT visible in the Admin Panel Audit tab until a later migration adds the action to
  the timeline function's allowlist (`ADMIN_AUDIT_ACTIONS_*`); until then they are in `core.audit_log` only.
  The X1.1 "Security audit events" card (dropped failed-login audit events: durable total, this API process's count,
  last backlog reading; a warning when anything was dropped or the total cannot be read) is kept on the reworked page
  as one more read-only indicator (`auditEvents`, a single Redis `GET` of the drop counter, bounded like every probe).

## XP-09 Q2/Q3 — Worker auth cleanup steps are isolated and drain the backlog in bounded batches (branch fix/worker-auth-cleanup-loop, 2026-11-13, PR #131)
- **Threat:** a failure in the refresh-token cleanup (e.g. the XP-09 23503) stopped the whole cycle, so the OAuth sign-in
  state cleanup after it never ran and rows holding provider e-mails were kept past their retention; and at most one batch
  of 1,000 rows per day meant a busy deployment never caught up.
- **Control:** the two steps (`auth-tokens` = core.worker_cleanup_auth_tokens, `oauth-transaction-state`) run isolated: a
  failing step is recorded with its step name and a SQLSTATE only (nothing else from the error), the other step still runs,
  then each failure is logged with a fixed message and reported through the existing failure path (no error text, no
  e-mails). Each step calls its function again until a batch comes back short; every call is its own autocommit
  transaction; the whole run is capped at 20 batches or 60 s, with one batch reserved for every later step so the OAuth
  cleanup always gets to run.
- **Residual:** refresh and password-reset tokens are deleted by one SQL function and cannot be isolated from each other
  without an SQL change. A run can outlast the 30 s Worker shutdown drain; only the in-flight batch rolls back.
- **Tests:** `token-cleanup.job.spec.ts` (isolation, fixed-text reporting, loop and caps on a fake clock),
  `token-cleanup-loop.integration.spec.ts` (5,000-row backlog drained in one run; a backlog above the cap stops at 20
  batches and finishes next run; a locked token table fails that step with 55P03 while OAuth rows are still deleted).

## DB-SETUP — database setup the Twenty Helm way: one database setting, crewflow_owner created by db-setup, a random password in a file (branch deploy/db-setup-like-twenty; owner-approved design 2026-11-13)

- **History.** 2026-11-12: one admin URL; a bootstrap child created `crewflow_owner` with a password derived from
  APP_SECRET (HKDF). 2026-11-13 option A, then option 2: the bootstrap moved into the one-shot `db-setup` service, and
  `PG_DATABASE_URL` became the one setting, given to db-setup only. Option 2 still derived the password from APP_SECRET
  and changed an existing `crewflow_owner`'s password. All of that is replaced by the Helm model below
  (`docs/plans/phase-x3/OWNER-DB-FINAL.md` Part A, `DB-SETUP-HELM-PLAN.md`): the HKDF derivation, the APP_SECRET rotation
  procedure, the derive/print commands, the owner-path password change and the strict-provider text are gone.
- **Install.** Bundled database: set `PG_DATABASE_PASSWORD` and `APP_SECRET`, then `docker compose up`. Your own
  database: put its admin URL, or an existing `crewflow_owner` URL, in `PG_DATABASE_URL` (compose.env). Nothing else: no
  SQL, no `psql`, no setup command, no second variable.
- **Change (Helm model).** `PG_DATABASE_URL` reaches the one-shot `db-setup` service only; rab-api and rab-worker pin it
  to `""` and refuse any value (exit 64). db-setup no longer receives APP_SECRET.
  - Bundled db or an admin URL, first start: db-setup generates a random 32-byte password and writes it atomically to the
    password file `/run/crewflow/db-target/owner-password` on the setup volume (0400, owner 1000:1000) BEFORE its transaction; then creates
    `crewflow_owner` only if it is missing (the `01-crewflow-owner.sql` attributes and grants). Later starts: the file
    exists and logs in, nothing changes.
  - An existing `crewflow_owner` URL: O1 and the read-only refusals only; the URL's password is copied into the file. The
    database is never written to and the password is never changed.
  - rab-api and rab-worker mount the setup volume read-only and build the `crewflow_owner` URL from `target.json`
    (host, port, database, TLS; no credential) and the password file. They wait (bounded, 120 s) for both, then exit 75.
  - A crash leaves either nothing in the database (the next start reuses the file) or a matching role: the file is written
    before the transaction.
- **Like Twenty** (`twentyhq/twenty` `main` @ `eedb0a73`, Helm chart). Only the setup step holds the admin credential, and
  only for the bundled database (`packages/twenty-docker/helm/twenty/templates/deployment-server.yaml:81-130`); it creates the user if missing and
  never changes an existing user's password (`:99-116`); the app password is random, kept apart and reused on upgrades
  (`.../templates/secret-db-url.yaml:3-8`); the server and worker receive only the app user's URL
  (`deployment-server.yaml:142-156`, `deployment-worker.yaml:76-90`); an external database is used as given
  (`secret-db-url.yaml:24-30`, `_helpers.tpl:56-83`). APP_SECRET is never part of a database credential, in Twenty or here.
- **Crewflow additions (not in Twenty; labelled per OWNER-DB-FINAL A4).**
  - **A client's admin URL → db-setup creates `crewflow_owner`.** Twenty would run the app as that login (superuser by
    default). Crewflow's tenant isolation needs RLS, which a superuser or BYPASSRLS login skips, so the app must run as
    `crewflow_owner`.
  - **Password file lost + admin URL → db-setup sets a new password** (new random password → file → `ALTER ROLE
    crewflow_owner PASSWORD`, Q4c). With Twenty, a lost secret leaves the app unable to log in. The admin login needs
    CREATEROLE and ADMIN OPTION on `crewflow_owner` (or superuser), else db-setup refuses (64) and names the fix. db-setup
    logs `crewflow_owner is ready (password reset because the password file was missing (Crewflow addition))`.
- **Refusals (exit 64, fixed message, nothing written).**
  - The password file exists but does not log in (for example the password was changed in the database): `"The stored crewflow_owner password does not log in. Delete the password file and start again with the admin address in PG_DATABASE_URL. Refusing."` (security review L1: neutral wording). No
    automatic reset (as Twenty: the existing user is skipped).
  - An admin URL names a database that does not exist: `"The database named in PG_DATABASE_URL does not exist (SQLSTATE 3D000). db-setup never creates a database: create it at your provider (the bundled db creates its own), then start again. Refusing."`. db-setup never creates a database (the bundled one
    is created by the postgres image, `POSTGRES_DB`).
  - Kept from option 2 (Crewflow has RLS, Twenty has not; OWNER-DB-FINAL A5): a `crewflow_owner` that is SUPERUSER,
    BYPASSRLS, REPLICATION or CREATEDB, has privileged memberships or lacks the required grants; PostgreSQL below 16; an
    admin that cannot create roles or grant; the H1 / N1 / N2 ownership and `search_path` refusals (TM-DB-3).
- **APP_SECRET never touches the database.** Changing it changes no database password and needs no database step.
- **Owner acceptance.** TM-DB-1, TM-DB-3, TM-DB-4 and T-1 to T-5 were accepted on 2026-11-12; the Helm model was approved
  by the owner on 2026-11-13 (OWNER-DB-FINAL Part A). TM-DB-2 below is new with it.

### TM-DB-1 (accepted risk) — the database URL sits in db-setup's definition
- **Actor → action → consequence.** Anyone who can read the compose project / OpenShip service definition (compose.env,
  `docker compose config`), or run `docker inspect` on the `db-setup` container, reads `PG_DATABASE_URL` → with an admin
  URL, full control of the database (superuser on the bundled db, bypassing RLS, COPY ... PROGRAM inside the db
  container; owner / CREATEROLE on a managed one); with a `crewflow_owner` URL, the schema owner login.
- **Controls.** `PG_DATABASE_URL` is interpolated ONLY into db-setup (and `PG_DATABASE_PASSWORD` only into db-setup's
  default URL and the bundled db's `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`). rab-api and rab-worker pin it to `""`: it is not in their PID 1,
  a runtime process, a `docker exec` process or a health check. db-setup runs only the bootstrap child and exits; it holds
  no port and the same hardening as rab-api. The entrypoints refuse a non-empty `PG_DATABASE_URL` (64); in production the
  API, the Worker and the migrate child refuse a non-`crewflow_owner` login before connecting (`runtime-db-config.ts`
  `checkRuntimeLogin`). The gates (compose-owner-login, verify-image-compose static and `--environment`) refuse a non-empty
  or interpolated `PG_DATABASE_URL` on rab-api / rab-worker, a compose file that interpolates `${PG_DATABASE_URL...}` more
  than once, any database credential or postgres:// value anywhere in their definition, and require db-setup's exact
  shape. The compose.env lint refuses a former separated login, TLS below verify-full, a transaction pooler, a URL without
  a password, and `PG_DATABASE_ADMIN_URL`; `PG_DATABASE_URL` in database.env / runtime.env is refused. The bundled db is
  never published and sits on an internal network.
- **Measured.** Option A and option 2 (PostgreSQL 16, live stacks): no admin credential in any rab-api / rab-worker
  process, `docker exec` process, health check or container definition. The Helm model: NOT re-measured on a live stack in this docs change (the CODE agent updated the live harness scenarios for OWNER-DB-FINAL A6 in d43696f8).
- **Residual.** As Twenty: the deployment configuration (compose.env, db-setup's definition) must be protected like the
  database itself; who can read it is outside Crewflow.

### TM-DB-2 (SUPERSEDED 2026-11-18 by TM-DB-6: no password file any more) — the crewflow_owner password file on the setup volume
- **Actor → action → consequence.** Anyone who can read the setup volume (root on the host, `docker run -v` on it, a copy
  of a volume backup) reads the `crewflow_owner` password → the schema owner login (RLS is FORCED, but the owner can alter
  policies).
- **Controls.** The file is written atomically (temp file + rename), mode 0400, owner 1000:1000, by db-setup only;
  rab-api and rab-worker mount the volume read-only. It is never logged or printed, never in an env file, a compose
  variable or the image: the gates refuse a variable carrying the `crewflow_owner` password and any mount at the
  password-file path other than db-setup's volume (db-setup read-write, the apps read-only), and the image gate fails on
  any file under `/run/crewflow/db-target` in the image. Security review L3: the gates also refuse `volumes_from` on any
  service, a `secrets` / `configs` target under `/run/crewflow`, a bind whose host source is inside Docker's volume store
  (`/var/lib/docker/volumes/...`, rootless `~/.local/share/docker`), a `tmpfs` at or under `/run/crewflow/db-target`, and a
  rab-redis that is not `user: 999:<gid>`. Reading is strict (security review L2): opened `O_RDONLY|O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK`,
  then `fstat` on that descriptor must show a regular file of at most 4096 bytes owned by the reading uid with no
  group/other bit; an empty file, a symlink, a FIFO or a wrong owner/mode is refused (exit 64), never read as "missing".
  Writing loops until every byte is written, sets the mode on the descriptor (never a path-based chmod) and fsyncs the
  file and the directory. A lost file is replaced only through the pending file below. Runs never overlap on one volume
  (security re-review F1, R1/R2): db-setup.sh first takes the KERNEL lock `flock -n` on fd 9 (`.db-setup.flock` in the
  volume; a second run stops with exit 70 before it reads, deletes or writes any file; the kernel releases it however the
  holder dies, so nothing is guessed about staleness), and the child also takes a lock directory (`.db-setup.lock`, mkdir);
  under the kernel lock a leftover directory is taken over through a tombstone checked by inode, without it never. A
  pending file is promoted only when it still holds this run's password (constant-time byte compare; otherwise exit 70 and
  nothing is renamed). Before the lock, two runs on one volume could leave the apps' file on one password and the role on
  another. The gates also refuse every other path to the volume from an added service (security re-review F2): a second
  top-level name for it (`external` alias), a `driver_opts` bind, `pid`/`ipc`/`network_mode` sharing with db-setup,
  rab-api or rab-worker (or any `container:`), a bind of the Docker root or its ancestors, and an added service running as
  uid 0 or 1000. Re-check R3/R4/I4: uids are parsed as canonical decimals (`01000`, `00` refused); binds of Docker's
  actual root (`docker info` DockerRootDir), its ancestors and descendants, of anything under `/run` or `/var/run` and of any
  `*.sock` are refused; an added service must drop all capabilities, set no-new-privileges, use no host namespace, map no
  device, add no group and run with no group 0; no volume of the deployed model has driver options or a non-local driver;
  the password volume's Docker name is exactly `<project>_crewflow-db-target`. The password is random (32 bytes),
  not derived from anything, so an APP_SECRET leak gives no database login. The bundled db is reachable only from the app network; an external database
  only through the provider's allow-list; verify-full TLS.
- **Residual.** Volume backups and snapshots contain the password: protect and encrypt them like the database. The file
  is plaintext at rest (T-9). Changing it on purpose: stop rab-api and rab-worker, remove `owner-password` and any pending
  `owner-password.next` with a one-off, environment-free `docker run` of the current image on the volume, `up -d` (the A4 reset; runbook section 7; not yet run live). Running apps do not pick up a new password on their own:
  their new connections fail with 28P01 until they are recreated, hence the stop.
- **Crash or failure during an A4 reset (security review L1, fixed).** db-setup stores the NEW password exclusively as the
  pending file `owner-password.next` before its transaction, and renames it over `owner-password` only after the COMMIT
  and a successful login with it. A run that fails in between (a crash, a Q4c error such as 22023, a lost connection)
  leaves `owner-password` untouched. The next start settles the pending file first: it logs in (the transaction had
  committed) -> promoted; 28P01 (nothing committed) -> deleted, and the normal path runs (A4 again when `owner-password`
  is missing); any other error -> exit 70 with the pending file kept. The apps read only `owner-password`. The stale-file
  refusal (`passwordFileStale`, exit 64) is now reached only when the stored password really does not log in.
- **Residuals after the third re-check (accepted, recorded).**
  - The apps' start wait is bounded by a COUNT (60 derive attempts, 2 s apart), so its real worst case is
    60 x (a cold `node` start + 2 s): about 2.5 min on an idle host, up to about 12 min if a cold start takes 10 s under load.
    The derive step itself has no external timer (busybox `timeout` held the fd-4 pipe for its whole bound); a FIFO, a
    symlink or a directory in place of a file is refused at once (O_NONBLOCK|O_NOFOLLOW + fstat), but a filesystem that
    hangs below `open` is not bounded (optional I1, an in-process watchdog with async reads, not done).
  - The derive step writes the URL only to an fd 4 its caller declared (`CREWFLOW_RUNTIME_URL_FD=4`, set only by
    api-prestart.sh / worker-start.sh and the documented operator command) and that is a pipe or a socket.
  - A run started WITHOUT db-setup.sh (development, the live harness) has no kernel lock; if it is killed it leaves
    `.db-setup.lock`, which is never taken over automatically (the message says to remove it when no db-setup runs).
  - `db` is in LOCAL_DATABASE_SERVICE_HOSTS (the bundled database's service name, as `devdb`/`postgres`/`pg`): non-production
    processes and DB_TARGET=local|test commands treat an UNMARKED database on host `db` as local (no remote-unmarked
    refusal). The identity marker does not protect it either: it is optional in production (BC-11) and its migration is not
    approved for production, so a production bundled database is usually unmarked. What protects the production bundled
    `db` is reachability: it publishes no port and sits only on the internal `crewflow-db` network (gate-enforced), where
    only db-setup, rab-api and rab-worker are attached; a non-production process or command elsewhere cannot resolve or
    reach that `db`. Only an override that attaches another service to `crewflow-db` could, and the gates refuse that (the
    committed files' service list; in a deployed model an added service on `crewflow-db` is refused).
- **One Crewflow deployment per PostgreSQL cluster when using an admin URL (security review L4, owner-approved).** Roles
  are cluster-wide: two deployments on one cluster share the one `crewflow_owner`, and an A4 reset by one (its password
  file lost) would change the password the other uses. Before an A4 reset the admin session runs one read-only SELECT
  (Q2b: `pg_shdepend` rows of `crewflow_owner` in another database, or its ownership of / ACL entry on another database)
  and refuses (exit 64, `ownerInOtherDatabase`) before anything is stored or written. Live: a second database with a
  fresh setup volume is refused and the first deployment's password keeps working.

### TM-DB-3 (accepted; changed by the Helm model) — a bootstrap runs with admin rights on every `up` (db-setup)
- **Actor → action → consequence.** A bug in, or an attacker-controlled input to, the bootstrap child could misuse admin
  rights.
- **Controls.** Fixed SQL only; the only interpolated values are the database name (`%I`) and the SCRAM verifier (`%L`
  inside a DO block, delivered as a bind parameter and a transaction-local setting, never in statement text). It never
  changes an existing role's attributes. It writes only when `crewflow_owner` is missing (CREATE ROLE and the narrow
  grants, not `GRANT ALL`) or on the A4 reset (ALTER ROLE ... PASSWORD). It refuses (exit 64, fixed message) an existing
  `crewflow_owner` that is SUPERUSER, BYPASSRLS, REPLICATION, CREATEDB, NOLOGIN, NOINHERIT, expired, or a member of a
  privileged role; an admin that cannot create roles or grant on the database; and a server below PostgreSQL 16. It takes a
  transaction advisory lock (key 7165901520526864244), re-reads the facts under it, retries a lost race a bounded number of
  times (at most 3 attempts), re-verifies the result and re-probes the login after commit. It prints fixed text and
  SQLSTATE classes only, never a URL, password, verifier, host or database name. The plaintext password never reaches the
  server (a pre-hashed SCRAM verifier is sent); a superuser admin turns statement and parameter logging off for its session.
  The `crewflow_owner` URL path runs read-only statements only, on a session opened with
  `default_transaction_read_only=on` (security review I1, owner-approved: a write there fails with 25006).
- **Session pinning (security review H1, CVE-2018-1058 class).** A `crewflow_owner` that owns the database (directly or
  through an inherited role) could set a database-level `search_path` and plant an operator that the admin session's
  unqualified `=` would then run with admin rights. Every bootstrap connection is opened with the startup options
  `-c search_path=pg_catalog,pg_temp -c default_transaction_read_only=off` (they override role and database defaults), and
  the first statement of every session sets the same search_path again. The admin path refuses (64) before any write when
  `crewflow_owner` owns the database (directly or through ANY role membership, inherited or SET-only:
  `pg_has_role(..., 'MEMBER')`, re-review N2), or when a database-wide or `crewflow_owner`-level `search_path` default
  exists. Residual (re-review N1): every database that went through `transition-from-separated.sql` is owned by
  `rab_owner`, of which `crewflow_owner` is a member, so it must use the `crewflow_owner` URL, never the admin URL
  (runbook 5.4). Changing the database owner to make the admin URL work is not a supported fix.
- **Residual.** With a NON-superuser admin whose provider logs statements with bind parameters (`log_statement=all`,
  pgaudit with parameters), the SCRAM verifier, never the password, lands in the provider's log. A verifier does not allow
  a login; offline guessing of a random 256-bit password is infeasible. A provider that refuses pre-hashed passwords is
  refused (64): there is no plaintext path (owner decision D6).
- **Evidence.** The H1 / N1 / N2 scenarios ran live on PostgreSQL 16 and 18 before the Helm model (option 2 harness). The Helm-model
  harness scenarios (d43696f8: fresh, restart, lost file, stale file, missing database, crewflow_owner URL unchanged,
  refusals, H1, N1, N2) are listed under Tests; their live results are not recorded here.

### TM-DB-4 (accepted) — the bundled database password in the environment
- **Change.** `PG_DATABASE_PASSWORD` is the bundled db's superuser password, read by compose only: the db's
  `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` and the default admin URL. It reaches no rab-api / rab-worker variable (the gates refuse it on every
  service but db, and in database.env / runtime.env; api-prestart.sh, worker-start.sh and db-setup.sh refuse it if present).
- **Controls on the bundled db.** Digest-pinned official postgres image (Debian 16; 17 and 18 work with the same layout);
  999:999, read-only root, `cap_drop ALL`, no-new-privileges, no port, internal network. It makes its own CA and a server
  certificate for `db` on first start; the CA private key is deleted right after signing; the server key stays in the data
  volume (0600); the app mounts only the CA certificate, read-only. On every start its entrypoint writes the `pg_hba.conf`
  the server reads (`hba_file`): `local all all scram-sha-256` and `hostssl all all ... scram-sha-256` only, so every TCP
  login must use TLS and a password (a plain-TCP connection is refused), and even a process inside the db container needs
  the password. The gates refuse any other `pg_hba` content, a `POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD`, initdb arguments other than
  SCRAM-only, and any db environment key outside an exact allow-list, in the committed AND the deployed model.
- **Residual.** The superuser can log in over the internal network (needed by db-setup's bootstrap child; T-3).
- **Your own database (2026-11-17, Twenty's Helm `db.enabled: false`).** `CREWFLOW_BUNDLED_DB=0` in compose.env renders
  the bundled db with 0 replicas: no idle superuser server runs beside an external database any more (before, it ran idle
  with its own superuser password). `PG_DATABASE_PASSWORD` stays required by the render (Compose interpolates every
  service; the `:?` refusal stays fail-closed for the bundled default) but reaches no container. "Your own database" is
  one predicate everywhere: a parseable `PG_DATABASE_URL` whose host is not the bundled `db`. Abuse cases:
  - `0` without your own database (no `PG_DATABASE_URL`, or one that still names host `db`) is refused by the compose.env
    lint and by the `--environment` preflight (`staging/verify-image-compose.cjs`: "db.deploy.replicas is 0 (only 1, or
    0 with your own database in PG_DATABASE_URL)").
  - If it is forced anyway, it fails closed at start: db-setup cannot use the bundled db, so rab-api never starts. On a
    host where the db never ran, db-setup refuses with exit 64 because the CA file is missing (verified live
    2026-11-17). Where an older `crewflow-db-ca` volume still holds a CA, it gets past that check and fails on connect
    (no `db` to reach), which is still a non-zero exit before rab-api.
  - Any value but `0` or `1` is refused by the lint.
  - The gate (committed model) and the preflight (deployed model) refuse a db replica count other than 1 (0 only with
    your own database), `scale`, or any other change to the `deploy` section.
  db-setup, the target files and every other control are unchanged in that mode.

### Trade-offs applied (SECURITY TRADE-OFF blocks; T-1 to T-5 owner-accepted 2026-11-12; T-9 follows the owner's Helm-model decision 2026-11-13)
- **T-1 — privileged URL in a container definition, db-setup's only.** The compose.env lint accepts a provider-admin login
  in `PG_DATABASE_URL`, which reaches db-setup only; it still refuses the former separated logins and schema roles, TLS
  below verify-full, a transaction pooler and a URL without a password. rab-api / rab-worker carry `""` only. Residual:
  TM-DB-1.
- **T-2 — `POSTGRES_PASSWORD` from an environment variable** on the bundled db, in both compose files (decision D4;
  OpenShip has no secret files). Residual: visible in the compose config / `docker inspect db`.
- **T-3 — the superuser may log in over the internal network** on the bundled db, only from db-setup's bootstrap child
  in practice (no other service holds its password), and only over TLS with SCRAM (`hostssl`). Still: no port, an
  internal network. Not narrowed to db-setup's address: pg_hba cannot name a compose service reliably.
- **T-4 — not applied** (D1 = a: verify-full kept for the bundled db; no plaintext exception).
- **T-5 — retired.** rab-api / rab-worker never receive any database URL; the entrypoints build the `crewflow_owner` URL
  from the target file and the password file and refuse any non-empty `PG_DATABASE_URL`; a runtime started any other way
  still refuses a non-`crewflow_owner` login in production before connecting.
- **T-6 — closed by the Helm model.** db-setup reads `database.env` only, never `runtime.env`, so it receives no APP_SECRET
  and no runtime secret; `db-setup.sh` refuses APP_SECRET (exit 64) and the gates refuse it on db-setup.**
- **T-7 — the API's wait is on the files only.** api-prestart.sh waits (120 s) for db-setup's target file and password
  file, not for a successful login; db-setup writes the target only after the role is ready. A start that finds a file but
  cannot log in is refused and restarted by Docker; it never takes an admin path.
- **T-9 (Helm model; follows the owner's decision OWNER-DB-FINAL Part A) — the `crewflow_owner` password at rest in
  plaintext in the setup volume file.**
  - Control relaxed: the password is stored unencrypted in `/run/crewflow/db-target/owner-password` (0400, uid 1000).
  - Who can read it: root on the host or anyone with Docker access (the volume, `docker cp`, a backup), and a process inside
    rab-api, rab-worker or db-setup (`docker exec`), which run as uid 1000.
  - Why: the owner chose the Twenty Helm model; this is the same class as Twenty's Kubernetes secret
    (`secret-db-url.yaml:3-8`), which is also readable by whoever controls the cluster.
  - What still holds: never in an env file, a compose variable, the image or a log; the apps mount it read-only; the gates
    refuse other mounts at that path and a variable carrying it (TM-DB-2).
  - Veto options: an encrypted file (needs a second secret to decrypt it, which then has the same exposure), or Docker
    secrets (OpenShip has no secret files).
- **OpenShip.** OpenShip discards `depends_on` conditions: `service_completed_successfully` is NOT VERIFIED there. The API
  does not rely on it: it waits, bounded, for the files and refuses (exit 75) without them.
- **Deployment identity (lead decision 2026-11-12): `db` joins `LOCAL_DATABASE_SERVICE_HOSTS`.** Outside production, an
  unmarked database at the single-label host `db` is treated as local (warn and continue). Production is unaffected.
  Residual: a non-production process whose `db` resolves through a DNS search domain to a remote database is not refused
  for a missing marker.
- **Owner CLI one-off authority.** With arguments, `api-prestart.sh` takes `DB_TARGET` / `ALLOW_PRODUCTION_DB_COMMANDS`
  out of its environment before its refusal loops and hands them back only to the one-off command; an API start without
  arguments still refuses both.

### Open follow-up (pre-existing, NOT fixed here) — finding B (area 6, Low)
A migrate child started with a `crewflow_owner` that is SUPERUSER is refused (exit 67, "the login is SUPERUSER"), but
before the refusal its DataSource has already created the `uuid-ossp` and `citext` extensions (owned by that login).
Root cause: the identity gate runs after the TypeORM DataSource initialise. In the deploy compose files db-setup refuses
such a role before any write and rab-api never starts, so this is reachable only by a migrate child started some other
way. A separate follow-up (fail-closed ordering in the migrate child) is for the owner.

### Upgrade hazard (PR #125 review, finding 3) — a `database.env` URL is silently overridden
`docker-compose.image.yml` commits `PG_DATABASE_URL: ""` on rab-api / rab-worker and `${PG_DATABASE_URL:-<bundled db>}` on
db-setup (which also reads database.env), and a compose `environment:` value wins over `env_file`: an existing deployment
that upgrades with `PG_DATABASE_URL` still in `database.env` connects to the new, empty bundled `db` and fresh-installs
there (its real database is untouched; the service runs empty, and a declared deployment identity is auto-bound to the new
database, which the plan's fresh-install rule allows). Not refused in code: the container only ever sees the winning
value, and refusing a fresh install on the bundled `db` would need a new rule that also blocks a legitimate first install.
Controls: the runbook's explicit upgrade step (3.2 step 0: move the line to `compose.env` before `pull`);
`compose-owner-login.cjs --lint-env-file database` and the `verify-image-compose.cjs --environment` preflight both refuse a
`database.env` that holds `PG_DATABASE_URL`; a `PG_EXPECTED_DATABASE_NAME` other than `crewflow` (the bundled db's name)
makes every process refuse the bundled database. Residual: an operator who skips the lint and the preflight, with no
`PG_EXPECTED_DATABASE_NAME` or one equal to `crewflow`.

### TM-DB-5 (owner-approved 2026-11-17) — your own database, app login created by you (`own-database-app-login.sql`)

A database admin creates `crewflow_owner` by hand with
`packages/rab-docker/postgres-init/owner-login/own-database-app-login.sql`. Crewflow then receives only the
`crewflow_owner` URL and never an admin credential (runbook OWNER-LOGIN-DEPLOYMENT.md section 4a; Twenty: an external
database, no setup step).

- **Owner decision 2026-11-17.** The SQL is approved, with two required steps:
  - the login test (runbook 4a step 3) before any variable is set or anything is deployed;
  - `ALTER ROLE crewflow_owner NOCREATEROLE` after the first start has completed: the rab-api log shows the migrate
    result with serve=true, or a restart reports state CURRENT (step 6).

  Owner 2026-11-17: both trade-offs accepted. The verifier can appear in logs (Twenty's Helm setup puts the plaintext
  password in SQL, so ours is stricter). The empty-password risk is caught by the required login test.

- **Result.** The role attributes and the database grant are identical to db-setup's Q4c. When a non-superuser admin
  creates it, the admin keeps the PostgreSQL 16 ADMIN-only creator row on `crewflow_owner`, the same row the db-setup
  admin path leaves. Rule 3 of the posture check accepts that row, and it gives the admin no INHERIT or SET.
- **Reduces TM-DB-1, from admin to schema owner; removes TM-DB-3 for this install.** db-setup's definition holds the
  `crewflow_owner` URL instead of an admin URL: whoever reads it gets the schema owner (with CREATEROLE until the
  hardening below), not the provider admin. No bootstrap runs with admin rights on `up`; db-setup's owner-URL mode is
  read-only.
- **Residual L2: the SCRAM verifier.** `\password` sends `ALTER USER crewflow_owner PASSWORD '<SCRAM verifier>'` as
  statement text. The verifier (not the password) can appear in server logs (log_statement ddl/all, or any failed
  ALTER), pg_stat_statements and audit logs. With verify-full TLS it is only an offline-guessing target, which a 32-byte
  random password defeats.
  - Proven on PG16 (2026-11-17): `pg_stat_statements` (track_utility on, the default) stores the full statement text,
    verifier included (`ALTER USER crewflow_owner PASSWORD 'SCRAM-SHA-256$4096:...'`). It is not normalised.
  - Control: the script runs db-setup's Q1 first. For a superuser admin it turns off this session's statement logging;
    proven: 0 verifier lines in a `log_statement=all` log. For a non-superuser admin Q1 is a no-op, and the log kept 1
    verifier line. Q1 does not affect pg_stat_statements or provider audit logs.
  - Control: the runbook requires `openssl rand -hex 32`. Not prevented: a weak password chosen by the admin.
  - db-setup avoids all of this with bind parameters inside a DO block, which psql cannot do. The exception is
    `log_statement=all` with a non-superuser admin, where PostgreSQL logs the bound parameter.
- **Residual M1: a partial or interactive run.** The script is meant to run as a file (`psql -X -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -f`).
  It also sets `ON_ERROR_STOP` on, `ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK` off and `AUTOCOMMIT` on itself, and every check runs inside the one
  transaction. A failed check therefore aborts the transaction even if psql keeps going, and COMMIT rolls back.
  - Proven: the file fed on stdin, a psqlrc with `ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK on` and `ON_ERROR_STOP off`, and the script with its
    `\set` lines removed all left no `crewflow_owner` on a cluster where `rab_owner` existed.
  - Not prevented: someone who pastes only some of the statements, or sets `ON_ERROR_ROLLBACK on` after the script's own
    `\set` lines. The runbook says never to paste it.
- **Residual L1: an empty or failed password entry.** `\password` runs inside the transaction. When the script is run as
  a file, mismatched entries stop psql and roll everything back (proven). An empty entry (two empty lines, or end of
  input) is accepted by psql, and the server then clears the password.
  - A failed `\password` in an interactive session (pasted, or `\i` then a manual COMMIT) can leave a role without a
    password; step 3 catches it.
  - A superuser admin: the re-check reads `pg_authid` and rolls back (proven).
  - A non-superuser admin cannot read `pg_authid`. The script then commits a passwordless LOGIN CREATEROLE role. It
    cannot log in with a password (proven: 28P01), and db-setup refuses it (exit 64). The runbook's login check names
    this state and its remedy (`REVOKE ... CASCADE; DROP ROLE crewflow_owner`, proven as the same admin).
  - Residual: such a role is usable only through a `trust`, `peer` or `cert` rule in the provider's `pg_hba.conf`.
